scope: The foreign donors to Indian associations as institutions — Ford Foundation, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Open Society Foundations, Omidyar Network India, USAID and the CEPPS consortium, Christian Aid, the Rockefeller and MacArthur foundations, and the two US diaspora charities named in the Hindutva-funding reports (Sewa International USA, IDRF) — with their identity, India footprint, published scale (IRS 990-PF where a page was opened) and the documented state actions against them (2015 Ford watch-listing and 2016 delisting; 2016 OSF prior-reference listing and the 2025 ED FEMA searches; the 2023 Omidyar exit; the February 2025 USAID 'US$21m voter turnout' episode). It then calibrates six circulating narratives about foreign money in Indian civil society against that record and against the domestic-philanthropy control (Bain 2025 aggregates; Tata Trusts). It leaves out: the FCRA enforcement register (research/raw/ngo/fcra-actions.json), donor-by-donor FC-4 receipts (fcra-receipts.json), and Compassion International / World Vision, which those files carry. Persons are recorded only where an office-holder is the counterparty of a documented act (the 2019 Gates award to the Prime Minister). George Soros and Bill Gates are not nodes: the institutions are.

claims.lab: Ford Foundation placed in prior-approval category and on MHA watch list
claims.d: 2015-04-23: MHA put Ford Foundation under the 'prior approval category' and on its watch list 'in the interest of national security', directing RBI under s.46 FCRA 2010 to bring all Ford remittances to its notice; stated ground: grants to Teesta Setalvad's Sabrang Trust/CJP allegedly not used for stated purposes. With Ford, 16 foreign donors were under the category. Setalvad denied the charge; MHA asked CBI to probe.

benefit.how: Case-by-case veto over one of the largest foreign grant-makers' remittances without a cancellation order

claims.upgradeIf: MHA order/RBI circular of April 2015 opened

claims.lab: Ford Foundation's position
claims.d: Foundation's standing statement: New Delhi office is a branch office with RBI/FEMA permission; all Indian grantees are FCRA-regulated and all grants FCRA-compliant; 'steadfast commitment to nonpartisanship'. Per Deccan Chronicle, Ford 'took up the matter with the Home Ministry' and was asked to register under FEMA, which it had not done since 1952.

claims.lab: Ford Foundation removed from prior-reference category
claims.d: 2016-03-18: MHA spokesperson — Ford removed from the prior reference category 'with immediate effect'; RBI asked to inform banks; remittances no longer need MHA clearance. Timing: ahead of the Prime Minister's US visit. Ford had by then been asked to register its liaison office under FEMA.

benefit.how: Restored unrestricted remittance capacity after eleven months

claims.lab: Global Goalkeeper Award 2019 for Swachh Bharat Abhiyan
claims.d: 2019-09-24, New York (UNGA sidelines): Gates Foundation conferred its Global Goalkeeper Award on the Prime Minister for the Swachh Bharat Mission ('over 500 million people… did not have access to safe sanitation, and now, the majority do' — foundation statement to NPR). Opposed beforehand by a petition of >100,000 signatures delivered to the foundation in Seattle and a letter co-signed by three Nobel Peace laureates citing Kashmir and 2002; foundation proceeded, saying the award was for 'the progress India is making in improving sanitation'. Non-monetary.

claims.lab: Was the Omidyar exit caused by enforcement pressure?
claims.d: Three candidate causes co-occur: (i) the stated market-maturity reason; (ii) 2022 CBI/FCRA scrutiny and the wider post-2020 FCRA tightening; (iii) 2023 portfolio write-downs (Doubtnut, ZestMoney). Insiders doubted 'several months of deliberation' because five investments had just been announced. The record cannot rank these; the exit is consistent with all three.
claims.innocentReading: A global impact investor closing a 13-year country programme after the local VC market matured and its own returns disappointed is ordinary portfolio strategy; Omidyar Network has exited other geographies without any enforcement context.
claims.upgradeIf: Internal board memo or a named executive attributing the exit to FCRA/CBI pressure
claims.killIf: Omidyar Network publishes a portfolio-return rationale with dates predating the CBI scrutiny

claims.lab: USAID government-to-government projects in India — FY2023-24 obligation
claims.d: US$97 million obligated in FY2023-24 (≈₹825 crore, the Finance Ministry annual report's own conversion, ≈₹85/US$) under seven ongoing projects with a total budget of about US$750 million (≈₹6,375 crore at the same rate), in food, agriculture, rural development, energy and environment — per the Finance Ministry annual report 2023-24 as reported by PTI. The annual report itself was not opened.

benefit.how: Grant finance to Union ministries' programmes

claims.upgradeIf: DEA annual report 2023-24 chapter on bilateral assistance opened

claims.lab: 'US$21 million for voter turnout in India' (DOGE/Trump claim)
claims.d: US$21m ≈ ₹178.5 crore at ₹85/US$ (rate implied by the FinMin annual-report conversion quoted by PTI; RBI reference rate for 2025-02 not fetched). 2025-02-16: DOGE's X post listed US$486m of USAID grants to CEPPS including 'US$21M for voter turnout in India', cancelled. Trump in Miami: 'Why do we need to spend $21 million for voter turnout in India?… I guess they were trying to get somebody else elected.' The asserting party is the US executive; no document showing an India grant was produced.
claims.upgradeIf: USAID/CEPPS award document naming India as the recipient country
claims.killIf: USAID award records show the only US$21m CEPPS voter-participation grant was for Bangladesh (see c017)

claims.lab: CEPPS/USAID response to the 'India voter turnout' label
claims.d: No response recorded — asked/not asked unknown
claims.upgradeIf: CEPPS or IFES/IRI/NDI public statement located

claims.lab: CEPPS US$21m 'Amar Vote Amar'/Nagorik — Bangladesh, 2022–2024
claims.d: US$21m ≈ ₹178.5 crore at ₹85/US$ (see c015 for rate basis). Indian Express investigation (2025-02-21), as carried by Business Standard: the only ongoing US$21m USAID–CEPPS voter-participation grant was sanctioned 2022-07 for Bangladesh, implemented by IFES, IRI and NDI ahead of the January 2024 election; US$13.4m disbursed by cancellation; USAID records show no CEPPS project in India since 2008. This is the record that contradicts c015.

benefit.how: Programme funding for Bangladesh civic-engagement events

claims.upgradeIf: USAspending.gov award record for the CEPPS Bangladesh agreement opened
claims.killIf: A separate India-designated CEPPS award of US$21m surfaces

claims.lab: MEA: USAID revelations 'deeply troubling'; agencies 'looking into this matter'
claims.d: 2025-02-21 weekly briefing, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal: 'We have seen information… put out by the US administration regarding certain USAID activities and funding. These are obviously very deeply troubling. This has led to concerns about foreign interference in India's internal affairs. Relevant departments and agencies are looking into this matter'; 'premature to make a public comment'. Asked about the Indian Express finding that the money went to Bangladesh, he did not engage. No outcome of the 'looking into' has been announced as of 2026-09-26 (not found).
claims.upgradeIf: MEA/MHA statement of findings

claims.lab: The same lens on the Government: USAID money to GoI dwarfs any alleged NGO election money
claims.d: If foreign money implies foreign influence, the FY2023-24 record shows US$97m obligated to Government of India projects (₹825 cr) against zero documented USAID election money to Indian associations. The 'foreign hand' lens, applied symmetrically, points at the state's own bilateral portfolio, which nobody in the controversy called interference.
claims.innocentReading: Government-to-government development assistance is negotiated, audited and reported by the DEA; it is categorically different from covert election funding, and its size says nothing about impropriety on either side.
claims.upgradeIf: n/a — comparison of documented figures
claims.killIf: DEA figures shown to include election-related programming

claims.lab: IB report (2014-06-03) names Greenpeace among 'anti-developmental' networks
claims.d: The 21-page report, first excerpted by the Indian Express and summarised by The News Minute, names Greenpeace with NAPM, PUCL and PMANE as coordinating anti-nuclear agitation, describes 'massive efforts… to take down India's coal fired power plant and coal mining activities', says Greenpeace is 'mainly against Coal India Ltd, Hindalco, Aditya Birla group and Essar', and opens with an unsourced estimate that such activity costs 2–3% of GDP growth. Commissioned under UPA, delivered to the NDA government.

benefit.how: The report frames campaigners against coal, POSCO and Vedanta projects as a security problem; the named project sponsors benefit if the framing is acted on

claims.upgradeIf: The report itself is published or tabled

claims.lab: Greenpeace rejects the IB report
claims.d: 2014-06-11 (IANS): Greenpeace India rejected the IB report and 'swears by energy sustainability'; the BHRRC timeline records its then executive director noting the coincidence of the leak with MHA action (2014-06-17 item).

claims.lab: The 2–3% of GDP figure has no traceable method
claims.d: The report's headline number is asserted without a source or method (The News Minute); the financial data it does cite are FCRA-reported (i.e., lawful) receipts. A figure of this size — comparable to India's entire annual public health budget share — attributed to seven agitations is not reproducible from any published estimate.
claims.innocentReading: Intelligence assessments are not economic papers; the number may be a rhetorical order-of-magnitude for project delays (POSCO, Kudankulam, Vedanta) that did impose real costs, and its authors never intended publication.
claims.upgradeIf: IB or MHA publishes the underlying estimate
claims.killIf: A published cost-of-delay study reaches a comparable figure by transparent method

claims.lab: IDRF disbursements reached Sangh-affiliated organisations (Sabrang/SACW 2002)
claims.d: Amount not stated in the section opened. The report's §4 argues that IDRF has 'well established links with the Sangh' and analyses donor-designated and IDRF-designated funds to show the bulk went to Sangh-affiliated recipients (Vanvasi Kalyan Ashram, Sewa Bharati, Ekal-type schools) for education, tribal and cultural work. The widely quoted '83% to Sangh affiliates' figure appears in secondary summaries and was not read in the primary text here. Asserting parties: Sabrang Communications and SACW.

benefit.how: US tax-deductible dollars to affiliates' service programmes

claims.upgradeIf: IDRF 990 schedules for 1994–2000 with recipient list opened and matched to Sangh affiliates
claims.killIf: Recipient list shows a majority of non-Sangh grantees

claims.lab: IDRF and Hindutva-side rebuttal
claims.d: Hindu Vivek Kendra published 'An analysis of the report The Foreign Exchange of Hate' by Ashok Chowgule disputing the report's characterisation; secondary accounts record IDRF's own November 2002 denial that the allegations were 'pure concoction, untruthful and self contradicting' and a 2003 rebuttal by six Indian-American academics — neither primary text was opened here.
claims.upgradeIf: IDRF's 2002 statement or the 2003 academic rebuttal opened

claims.lab: Sewa International USA among seven US charities that spent US$158.9m (2001–19), part sent to Sangh-linked groups in India (Macher/SACW 2022)
claims.d: Amount not stated for Sewa alone. The pseudonymous 2022 report, as read by ThePrint, tallies at least US$158.9m spent by seven US charities 2001–2019 (US$85.4m in 2014–19), 'sending some of it to groups in India', and lists the Sangh affiliations of family-foundation donors; it concedes 'most of [the actions] are legal'. Asserting party: the report's author via SACW.

benefit.how: Diaspora charitable dollars to affiliates' service networks in India

claims.upgradeIf: Sewa International USA 990 Schedule F (foreign grants) opened and Indian recipients' FC-4 returns matched
claims.killIf: Schedule F shows recipients unconnected to Sangh affiliates

claims.lab: Sewa International USA response
claims.d: No response recorded — asked/not asked unknown
claims.upgradeIf: Sewa International USA statement located (HAF's 'baseless' statement is HAF's own, not Sewa's)

claims.lab: MHA's 2026 statement of what FCRA is for
claims.d: PIB factsheet 2026-07-22: FCRA 'identifies who may accept foreign contributions', 'specifies how that money must be received, accounted for, and reported', and 'restricts a narrow, defined set of foreign-funded activities that could affect India's sovereignty, security or public order'; 'What FCRA does not do is forbid Indians from receiving foreign donations or shut down law abiding civil society'; core objectives 'transparency, accountability, sovereignty, enabling genuine work'. This is the Government's own contra to narrative 2.

claims.lab: FCRA Amendment Rules 2026 — new disclosure, activity and functionary-liability conditions
claims.d: Notified 2026-06-22. ICNL: activity and geographic limitations, bars on foreign-national involvement, liability exposure for 'key functionaries', increased reporting, new spending/utilisation thresholds. Amnesty (2026-07-17): 'sweeping new powers to police the activities, operation, management and leadership' of NGOs. Applies to registered, renewing and prior-permission holders.
claims.upgradeIf: Gazette notification G.S.R. of 2026-06-22 opened

claims.lab: Aggregate FCRA cancellations cited by monitors
claims.d: Freedom House (2025): 'In 2022, the government said it had cancelled the FCRA registrations of 6,677 NGOs between 2017 and 2021'; April 2024 cancellations of CNI Synodical Board, VHAI, IGSSS, CASA and EFI 'citing improper use of foreign funding contributions'. HRW (2016): FCRA invoked against 25 groups; HRW (2022): calls the law's use 'abusive'. CIVICUS rates India 'Repressed' (30/100) every year 2019–2024 after 'Obstructed' in 2018. Detailed cancellation records are in fcra-actions.json.
claims.upgradeIf: MHA Parliament answer with year-wise cancellations and grounds (see sibling file)

claims.lab: Scale control: Indian private philanthropy ₹1.31 lakh crore (FY2024) vs the foreign-contribution channel
claims.d: Bain 2025: total social-sector funding ~₹25 lakh crore (8.3% of GDP), 95% public; private ~₹1,31,000 crore (US$16bn) in FY2024, growing 7%; family philanthropy ~40% of private giving; family-run firms' CSR ~₹18,000 crore. Foreign contribution (see fcra-receipts.json aggregates) is a small fraction of private giving and a rounding error against public spending — the denominator every 'foreign money' narrative omits.
claims.innocentReading: Bain's estimates are consultant aggregates (with Dasra), not audited flows; the comparison shows scale, not the political salience of particular foreign grants to advocacy groups, which can be high at small size.
claims.upgradeIf: FC-4 aggregate for FY2024 from MHA set against Bain's private-giving figure

narratives.claim: Foreign-funded NGOs are stalling India's development, costing 2–3% of GDP a year, as the 2014 Intelligence Bureau report showed.
narratives.strongestCase: The report exists (dated 2014-06-03, 21 pages, commissioned under UPA), was leaked within days of the new government taking office, and its thesis was acted on: within a year the MHA suspended Greenpeace India's registration, placed Ford and 15 other donors under prior reference, and cancelled thousands of lapsed registrations (see fcra-actions.json). Campaigns against Kudankulam, POSCO and Vedanta's Niyamgiri project did delay large investments, and some campaigners were foreign-funded.
narratives.strongestCounter: The 2–3% GDP figure is asserted without source or method (The News Minute); the financial data cited are lawful FCRA-reported receipts, with 'no mention of any money that has come through illegal means'. The report treats lawful protest, litigation and journalism (a documentary, a TISS study) as 'anti-developmental activity'. Greenpeace rejected it; a Delhi High Court later found the Greenpeace actions disproportionate (sibling file). The document has never been published or tabled, so the Government has used an assessment nobody can audit.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Publication of the report with its cost method; or a transparent cost-of-delay study; or evidence that named groups received undeclared (non-FCRA) money.

narratives.claim: FCRA is used to silence government critics.
narratives.strongestCase: Monitors across a decade record the pattern: HRW (2016) on 25 groups including Greenpeace, Sabrang, Navsarjan, INSAF; HRW (2022) calling the law's use 'abusive'; Freedom House scoring NGO freedom 2/4 and noting the power is 'used selectively against perceived political opponents'; CIVICUS 'Repressed' every year since 2019; Amnesty (2026) on the new Rules' 'sweeping powers'. The Ford episode shows the instrument at work: listed for funding a critic's NGOs, delisted before a PM visit to the US. HRW's 2016 finding is that 'successive governments' did this — the UPA's 2012 Kudankulam cancellations included.
narratives.strongestCounter: The Government's stated framing (PIB 2026): a registration-and-disclosure regime like those of the US, UK, Australia and Canada, restricting only 'a narrow, defined set' of activities; tens of thousands of associations remain registered. Most cancellations are for non-filing of returns, not politics (sibling file base rates); April 2024 cancellations hit church-linked service bodies (CASA, EFI, CNI), not government critics, on 'improper use' grounds. Courts have upheld the 2020 Amendment (Noel Harper, 2022). Government-aligned associations have also lost registration (sibling file).
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A year-wise MHA table of cancellations by stated ground and by the target's public orientation, showing critics are not over-represented after controlling for filing compliance; or, conversely, internal notes tying listings to speech.

narratives.claim: George Soros / the Open Society Foundations fund regime change in India.
narratives.strongestCase: The founder said in public (Munich, 2023-02-16) that Modi 'is no democrat', that the Adani affair 'will significantly weaken Modi's stranglehold on India's federal government', and 'I expect a democratic revival in India'. OSF has been under MHA prior reference since 2016 (reported), and in March 2025 the ED searched eight Bengaluru premises alleging OSF routed money as FDI and consultancy fees to bypass that restriction. OSF's global grant-making (FPOS + OSI expenses ≈US$757m in 2024) includes democracy and rights programmes. The BJP's response (Smriti Irani at party HQ, 2023-02-17) framed the remarks as an attack on India's democratic process.
narratives.strongestCounter: A wish stated at a security conference is not a funding programme; the speech contains no reference to OSF spending in India. No adjudicated finding — under FCRA, FEMA or the Representation of the People Act — has ever held that OSF financed Indian electoral or 'regime change' activity; the 2025 ED matter is an unadjudicated FEMA allegation from 'sources'. OSF's India spend is unpublished and, on the 2016 listing, every rupee to an FCRA association has needed MHA clearance for a decade. The narrative names a person and, in its common form, an ethnicity; the institutional record is a prior-reference listing and a search.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: An ED/adjudicating-authority order with quantified transfers to political or electoral activity; or OSF grant records to Indian entities engaged in electoral work; or, on the other side, a court quashing the FEMA proceedings.

narratives.claim: USAID paid US$21 million to raise voter turnout in India (to defeat the ruling party).
narratives.strongestCase: DOGE's 2025-02-16 list said so in terms; the US President repeated it ('trying to get somebody else elected'); the BJP's IT head called it 'external interference'; and the MEA said the revelations were 'very deeply troubling' and under examination — three official-level actors treating it as real.
narratives.strongestCounter: The only US$21m USAID–CEPPS voter-participation grant on record was sanctioned in 2022-07 for Bangladesh ('Amar Vote Amar', later Nagorik), implemented by IFES/IRI/NDI ahead of Bangladesh's January 2024 poll, with US$13.4m spent; USAID records show no CEPPS project in India since 2008 (Indian Express investigation, carried by Business Standard, The News Minute and others). The Finance Ministry's own annual report shows USAID's India money went to seven Government projects (US$97m obligated FY24). Neither Washington nor Delhi produced a document naming India; the MEA declined to engage with the Bangladesh finding and has announced no result. USAID itself was closed on 2025-07-01.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A USAID award document designating India as the recipient of election-participation funds; absent that, the claim stays debunked. An MEA statement of findings would settle the Indian side.

narratives.claim: Missionary NGOs use foreign money to convert Indians.
narratives.strongestCase: Christian charities and churches are among the largest declared foreign sources and recipients under FCRA (fcra-receipts.json: Compassion, LDS Church, Gospel for Asia, World Vision at the top of US-source lists); the MHA has cited religious grounds in actions against Compassion International (2017) and cancelled church-linked bodies (CASA, EFI, CNI Synodical Board in April 2024). Several states criminalise conversion by inducement, and the Government's 2026 Rules add 'activity limitations'.
narratives.strongestCounter: Receiving foreign money for religious purposes is lawful under FCRA — the Act's own categories include 'religious', and the PIB factsheet says the law does not 'forbid Indians from receiving foreign donations'. The documented 2024 cancellations cite 'improper use of foreign funding', not conversion. Christian Aid's India programme, for instance, is caste, governance and livelihoods work through 27 partners in 16 states. The narrative merges three distinct things — lawful faith-based welfare, lawful religious activity, and unlawful inducement — and the third has produced very few convictions. The same lens applied to Hindu diaspora charities (narrative 6) yields the same shape: religiously affiliated foreign money to religiously affiliated service networks.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Court convictions under state anti-conversion laws tied to specific FCRA-received funds; or, conversely, MHA data showing religious-purpose registrations are cancelled at the same rate as others.

narratives.claim: RSS affiliates receive foreign money through their US chapters (Sewa International, IDRF), as the 2002 Sabrang/SACW report and the 2019–22 Hindutva-funding reports showed.
narratives.strongestCase: That US 501(c)(3)s with Sangh-linked leadership raise tax-deductible dollars and remit them to Indian affiliates' schools, tribal-welfare and relief programmes is documented in the reports' own reading of IRS 990s: the 2002 report's §4 traces IDRF's disbursement pattern; the 2022 report tallies US$158.9m spent by seven groups over 2001–19 with part sent to India; five such groups received US$833,000 of US Covid relief (Al Jazeera 2021, per ThePrint). The affiliates' Indian recipients (Ekal Vidyalaya Foundation of India, Sewa Bharati, VKA) hold FCRA registrations and file FC-4s (fcra-receipts.json). Unlike Ford or OSF, no MHA prior-reference listing or cancellation is recorded against these donors.
narratives.strongestCounter: The flow is lawful and declared on both ends; the reports themselves say 'most of [the actions] are legal'. The characterisation — that the money 'funds hate' or violence — is the contested part: IDRF called the 2002 allegations 'pure concoction', six academics published a rebuttal (2003), HAF calls the 2022 report 'baseless' and its author is pseudonymous. The 83% figure is unverified here. Run symmetrically, the lens that treats Sangh-affiliated service work as political funding also treats church-affiliated service work as conversion funding (narrative 5) — the two narratives are mirror images, and neither has an adjudicated finding behind it.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Schedule F recipient lists of Sewa International USA and IDRF matched to FC-4 receipts of named affiliates would turn 'well-supported' to 'documented' for the flow; a finding by any tribunal that funds financed violence would change the characterisation.

symmetryCheck: Same lens on the controls. (1) Domestic philanthropy: Tata Trusts, Azim Premji Foundation, Reliance Foundation and Adani Foundation face no prior-permission gate, no watch list and no donor-wise disclosure of the FCRA kind; Bain puts private giving at ~₹1.31 lakh crore in FY2024 against a foreign-contribution channel that is a small fraction of it — so the regulatory attention is inversely proportional to scale. Their pages were not all retrievable, so their individual disbursements are a gap. (2) Government-aligned foreign donors: Sewa International USA and IDRF are documented (by their critics' reading of 990s) as remitting to Sangh-affiliated service networks, exactly as Ford, OSF and Christian charities remit to their grantees; the state acted against Ford (2015–16), OSF (2016→, 2025) and Compassion (2017) and has no recorded action against the Sangh-linked channel. Both sides' 'political intent' claims rest on inference from grantee ideology; neither has an adjudicated finding. (3) The Government itself: USAID's documented India money went to seven Union projects (US$97m FY24) — orders of magnitude more than any documented USAID money to Indian associations — and nobody called it interference. (4) The Gates Foundation, the largest foreign health donor with formal state MoUs and an award to the PM, has no recorded MHA action; the one large foreign donor treated as a partner is the one that does not fund rights advocacy. Finding about the lens: 'foreign money → foreign influence' produces an alarming picture of every side, including the state; what varies is whom the state chooses to apply it to.
